q: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
x: Au comes from the Latin word aurum, meaning gold. Silver's symbol, Ag, comes from the Latin argentum.

q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
x: Mercury orbits the Sun in just 88 Earth days, the shortest year of any planet.

q: Which gas do plants absorb from the air for photosynthesis?
x: Plants use sunlight to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

q: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance?
x: Diamond is a form of pure carbon whose atoms are locked in a rigid crystal lattice. It scores 10 on the Mohs scale.

q: How many bones are in the adult human body?
x: Babies are born with about 300 bones, and many of them fuse together as the child grows.

q: What is the chemical formula for water?
x: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. Adding a second oxygen gives hydrogen peroxide.

q: What force pulls objects toward the center of the Earth?
x: On Earth's surface, gravity makes falling objects accelerate at about 9.8 meters per second every second.

q: At sea level, at what temperature does water boil in degrees Celsius?
x: Water boils at lower temperatures at high altitude because the air pressure is lower, which is why cooking takes longer on mountains.

q: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
x: Mars looks red because its soil is rich in iron oxide, which is essentially rust.

q: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
x: Nitrogen is about 78 percent of the air we breathe, while oxygen is only about 21 percent.

q: What is the process by which plants make their own food using sunlight?
x: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in leaves, inside tiny structures called chloroplasts.

q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
x: The ampere is named after the French physicist Andre-Marie Ampere, a founder of the study of electromagnetism.

q: Which blood cells carry oxygen around the body?
x: Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that also gives blood its red color.

q: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
x: Na comes from natrium, the Latin name for sodium compounds. Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water.

q: What is Earth's only natural satellite?
x: The Moon is slowly drifting away from Earth at about 3.8 centimeters per year.

q: Which scientist is famously linked with a falling apple and the law of universal gravitation?
x: Newton published his law of universal gravitation in 1687 in his book Principia.

q: About how fast does light travel in a vacuum?
x: Light covers about 300,000 kilometers every second, fast enough to circle Earth about 7.5 times in one second.

q: At what temperature in degrees Celsius does water freeze at sea level?
x: Water expands when it freezes, which is why ice floats and why pipes can burst in winter.

q: Which gas do humans need to breathe in to survive?
x: Our cells use oxygen to release energy from food, a process called cellular respiration.

q: What is the scientific study of living things called?
x: The word biology comes from the Greek words bios (life) and logos (study).

q: Which planet is best known for its spectacular rings?
x: Saturn's rings are made mostly of chunks of water ice, ranging from dust grains to boulders.

q: What kind of animal is a dolphin?
x: Dolphins breathe air through a blowhole and nurse their young with milk, like all mammals.

q: What do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
x: A bee must visit about two million flowers to make one pound of honey.

q: Which part of a plant absorbs water from the soil?
x: Tiny root hairs greatly increase the surface area available for taking in water and minerals.

q: What is the common name for sodium chloride?
x: Salt is so valuable in history that the word salary is thought to come from the Latin word for salt.

q: Which vitamin does your skin make when exposed to sunlight?
x: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth.

q: How many legs does an insect have?
x: All adult insects have six legs and three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen.

q: How many colors are traditionally listed in a rainbow?
x: Newton chose seven colors, red to violet, partly because he linked them to the seven notes of the musical scale.

q: What is the tiny, dense center of an atom called?
x: The nucleus holds nearly all of an atom's mass, yet it is about 100,000 times smaller than the whole atom.

q: Which pair of organs filters waste from the blood to make urine?
x: Your kidneys filter about 180 liters of blood plasma every day.

q: What sound follows a flash of lightning?
x: Thunder is caused by the air being heated so fast that it expands explosively. Light travels faster than sound, so you see lightning first.

q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
x: Mercury's symbol, Hg, comes from the Latin hydrargyrum, meaning liquid silver.

q: Counting outward from the Sun, which planet is third?
x: Earth sits in the so-called habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid water on the surface.

q: What do we call animals that eat only plants?
x: Cows, rabbits and elephants are herbivores. Many have specialized stomachs to break down tough plant material.

q: What is the chemical symbol for oxygen?
x: Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of Earth's atmosphere and nearly half of the mass of Earth's crust.

q: Which force slows down a book sliding across a table?
x: Friction turns some of the sliding object's motion energy into heat, which is why rubbing your hands together warms them.

q: Which scientist wrote On the Origin of Species?
x: Darwin published the book in 1859 after developing his ideas on natural selection for over twenty years.

q: Which instrument is used to see distant stars and planets more clearly?
x: Galileo's improved telescopes in 1609 and 1610 let him see the Moon's craters and the moons of Jupiter.

q: What does the abbreviation DNA stand for?
x: DNA carries the genetic instructions for building and running living things, coiled into a double helix.

q: In computing, what does CPU stand for?
x: The CPU is often called the brain of the computer because it carries out program instructions.

q: What are the smallest units of digital information, the 0s and 1s, called?
x: The word bit is short for binary digit. Eight bits make up one byte.

q: Which type of rock forms when molten lava or magma cools and hardens?
x: Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks. The name comes from the Latin word for fire.

q: What is the name for molten rock beneath Earth's surface?
x: Magma is called lava once it erupts onto the surface.

q: What is the name of the thin, rocky outer layer of the Earth?
x: The crust is only 5 to 70 km thick, thinner relative to Earth than the skin of an apple is to the fruit.

q: What is mainly responsible for the ocean tides on Earth?
x: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, creating two tidal bulges. Most coasts see two high tides a day.

q: What is the longest bone in the human body?
x: The femur, or thigh bone, makes up about a quarter of a person's height.

q: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
x: Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin word for iron. Iron is the most common element on Earth by mass.

q: Roughly how many days does the Earth take to orbit the Sun once?
x: Because the orbit takes about 365.25 days, we add a leap day to the calendar roughly every four years.

q: Which planet has the hottest surface in the solar system?
x: Venus is hotter than Mercury, at about 465 C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat.

q: What is the SI unit of force?
x: One newton is about the weight of a small apple on Earth's surface.

q: What is a young frog with a tail and gills called?
x: A tadpole gradually grows legs, loses its tail and develops lungs in a process called metamorphosis.

q: What is it called when liquid water turns into water vapor?
x: Evaporation from oceans, lakes and plants drives the water cycle that eventually returns as rain and snow.

q: What is it called when water vapor cools and turns into liquid droplets?
x: Clouds form when water vapor condenses onto tiny dust particles in the air.

q: What does a seismograph record?
x: Modern seismographs can detect earthquakes happening on the opposite side of the planet.

q: What does a barometer measure?
x: Falling air pressure often signals approaching storms, while rising pressure usually means fair weather.

q: Which pair of organs do we use to breathe?
x: Your lungs contain around 300 million tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen enters the blood.

q: About how long does the Earth take to rotate once on its axis?
x: Earth's spin gives us day and night. At the equator, the ground moves at roughly 1,670 km/h.

q: What is a recognizable pattern of stars in the night sky called?
x: Astronomers recognize 88 official constellations, including Orion and Ursa Major.

q: Which part of a cell is known as its powerhouse?
x: Mitochondria convert food into ATP, the usable energy molecule of the cell. They have their own small set of DNA.

q: What green pigment in leaves captures sunlight for photosynthesis?
x: Leaves turn red and orange in autumn when chlorophyll breaks down and other pigments show through.

q: Which scientist won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry?
x: Curie won the Physics prize in 1903 and the Chemistry prize in 1911, and is the only person honored in two different sciences.

q: What is the largest animal on Earth?
x: A blue whale's heart is about the size of a small car, and its tongue can weigh as much as an elephant.

q: Which is the fastest land animal?
x: A cheetah can reach about 100 km/h in short bursts, accelerating faster than most sports cars.

q: Among the eight planets, which one is farthest from the Sun?
x: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.

q: Who invented the World Wide Web?
x: Berners-Lee proposed the web in 1989 while working at the research lab CERN in Switzerland.

q: Which element is the lightest in the universe?
x: Hydrogen is also the most abundant element in the universe and the main fuel of stars.

q: What word describes animals that are mainly active at night?
x: Owls, bats and many mice are nocturnal, with senses adapted for darkness.

q: Which state of matter has a fixed volume but no fixed shape?
x: A liquid takes the shape of its container, but you cannot easily squeeze it into a smaller volume.

q: What do paleontologists study?
x: Paleontologists piece together the history of life from fossils, some of them hundreds of millions of years old.

q: What object passes between the Sun and the Earth during a solar eclipse?
x: By coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and also about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size.

q: How many teeth does a typical adult human have, including wisdom teeth?
x: Children have 20 baby teeth, which are replaced by permanent teeth.

q: Which gas is used to fill party balloons so they float?
x: Helium is lighter than air. It was first detected in the Sun in 1868, before it was found on Earth.

q: What does a magnetic compass needle point toward?
x: Earth's liquid iron core generates a magnetic field that the needle aligns with.

q: Which vitamin, found in oranges and lemons, helps prevent scurvy?
x: Sailors on long voyages once suffered terribly from scurvy until citrus fruit was added to their diet.

q: What is the SI base unit of mass?
x: The kilogram is the only SI base unit with a prefix in its name.

q: Which natural disaster is the Richter scale used to measure?
x: Charles Richter developed his scale in 1935. Today scientists mostly use a related moment magnitude scale.

q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite launched into orbit in 1957?
x: Sputnik 1 was about the size of a beach ball and beeped radio signals for three weeks.

q: What is the process called by which a caterpillar changes into a butterfly?
x: Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body is largely broken down and rebuilt into the adult butterfly.

q: How many legs does a spider have?
x: Spiders are arachnids, not insects. They also have two body parts instead of three.

q: What is the layer of gases surrounding the Earth called?
x: Most of the atmosphere's mass sits within the lowest 16 km, the layer where weather happens.

q: What is the scientific study of weather called?
x: Meteorology has nothing to do with meteors. The name comes from a Greek word for things high in the sky.

q: Which organ controls the body's thoughts, memory and movement?
x: The human brain has roughly 86 billion nerve cells, called neurons.

q: What energy source do solar panels convert into electricity?
x: Solar cells use the photovoltaic effect, in which light knocks electrons loose in a semiconductor, usually silicon.

q: Which group of animals is the only one with feathers?
x: Feathers help birds fly, stay warm and attract mates. Their closest living relatives are the crocodiles.

q: What is the name of the famous space telescope launched in 1990?
x: Hubble orbits about 540 km above Earth, above the blurring effect of the atmosphere.

q: A ramp is an example of which simple machine?
x: An inclined plane lets you lift a heavy load with less force over a longer distance.

q: What is the huge explosion of a dying massive star called?
x: A supernova can briefly outshine an entire galaxy and scatters heavy elements like iron into space.

q: What is the basic building block of all living things?
x: The human body contains roughly 30 trillion cells of about 200 different types.

q: What is the hardest natural substance on Earth?
x: Diamond is pure carbon whose atoms are packed in a very strong crystal structure.

q: Which part of the eye changes the size of the pupil?
x: The colored iris has tiny muscles that open or close the pupil to control light.

q: What type of scientist studies rocks and the structure of the Earth?
x: Geologists read rock layers to learn how Earth has changed over millions of years.

q: Which planet is famous for its bright rings of ice and rock?
x: Saturn's rings are mostly water ice and stretch far wider than the planet itself.

q: What is the force that slows things down when surfaces rub together?
x: Friction turns movement into heat, which is why rubbing your hands warms them.

q: What state of matter is steam?
x: Steam is water that has been heated until it becomes a gas.

q: What is the process of water turning into vapor called?
x: Heat from the Sun makes water evaporate from oceans, lakes and puddles.

q: What is a sudden shaking of the ground called?
x: Earthquakes happen when blocks of Earth's crust slip along a fault.

q: Which vitamin can our skin make with the help of sunlight?
x: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones.

q: Which tool lets you see things too small for the naked eye?
x: Microscopes let scientists study cells and tiny organisms.

q: Which tool is used to look at distant stars and planets?
x: Galileo used an early telescope to see the moons of Jupiter.

q: What is frozen water called?
x: Water freezes into ice at 0 degrees Celsius.
